issues.legal_issue: A court exercising supervisory jurisdiction may not reappreciate evidence and substitute its own view for that of the statutory authorities.
material_facts: The statutory revisional authority set aside the appellate eviction order and restored the Rent Controller’s dismissal of the eviction petition.
In supervisory proceedings, the High Court reassessed the findings and substituted its own view, relying in part on a factual account that was contrary to the pleadings and evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by substituting its view for that of the statutory authority, and its order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 of the Constitution does not permit the High Court, while exercising supervisory jurisdiction over statutory rent-control authorities, to reappreciate the evidence and substitute its own judgment for the statutory authority’s judgment.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_rent_control_decis: A party sought supervisory review of a decision made by a statutory authority in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.high_court_reappreciated_evidence: The High Court reassessed evidence considered by the statutory authority.
predicates.high_court_substituted_its_view: The High Court replaced the statutory authority’s view with its own.

issues.definition: When a High Court reviewing a rent-control decision reappraises the evidence and replaces the statutory authority’s view with its own, its supervisory interference exceeds its jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking eviction for own occupation must establish an objectively genuine need, rather than a mere desire or an unsupported and inconsistent claim.
material_facts: The landlord sought the premises for residence and to conduct unspecified affairs, but later testified that he wanted to move his travel-agency business there.
The landlord was conducting that business from a room in a hotel, and the claimed need to move it was not stated in the eviction application or in his examination-in-chief.
The landlord gave changing explanations for needing the premises, including a threat to his existing accommodation and practical difficulties in running the business there.
The Rent Controller found that the premises were unsuitable for the stated business purpose, that the landlord had not faced an immediate need to shift, and that the claimed need was a pretext.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s bona fide need was not established, and the eviction order could not stand on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 11(3) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, a landlord seeking eviction for own occupation bears the burden of establishing a genuine requirement; mere desire is insufficient and the need must be assessed objectively. The Court relied on Mattulal v. Radhe Lal, (1974) 2 SCC 365.

rule.if: own_occupation_eviction_proceeding and landlord_bears_burden_of_proving_need and (claim_lacks_specific_particulars or explanations_are_inconsistent or asserted_purpose_is_not_supported_by_evidence)

predicates.own_occupation_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the ground that the landlord required the premises for own occupation.
predicates.landlord_bears_burden_of_proving_need: The landlord seeking eviction was responsible for establishing the claimed need.
predicates.claim_lacks_specific_particulars: The landlord did not give specific particulars of the purpose for which the premises were required.
predicates.explanations_are_inconsistent: The landlord gave changing explanations for why the premises were needed.
predicates.asserted_purpose_is_not_supported_by_evi: The evidence did not support the landlord’s asserted purpose for requiring the premises.

issues.definition: In an own-occupation eviction proceeding, when the landlord bears the burden of proving need and the claim lacks particulars, has inconsistent explanations, or lacks evidentiary support, bona fide need is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A claimed need founded on threatened acquisition is unavailable as a basis for eviction when the acquisition proceedings have lapsed or been abandoned.
material_facts: The landlord principally relied on an alleged immediate threat that another premises in his occupation would be acquired for a town-planning scheme.
By the time the appeal was considered, the acquisition proceedings were admitted to have been given up or to have lapsed through the passage of time.
issues.conclusion: The alleged acquisition threat was no longer available as the principal ground supporting the eviction application.
issues.legal_principle: A factual ground relied on to establish the need for eviction cannot support that claim when the asserted threat has ceased to exist; the Court applied this to the landlord’s own-occupation claim under Section 11(3) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act.

predicates.rent_control_own_occupation_eviction_pro: A landlord sought eviction in a rent-control proceeding on the basis of a need for own occupation.
predicates.claimed_need_rests_on_threatened_acquisi: The landlord relied on threatened acquisition of another premises as a reason for requiring the tenanted premises.
predicates.acquisition_proceedings_lapsed_or_were_a: The acquisition proceedings had lapsed or had been given up.

issues.definition: When an own-occupation eviction claim relies on threatened acquisition of another premises and those proceedings have lapsed or been abandoned, that acquisition-based need is unavailable.
